01先看 Lab3 開發規格與繳交項目

完成支援 37 條 RV32I 指令的單週期 CPU；實作九個 Verilog 模組，以參考 ISS 逐指令比對，最後繳交 report.md 與架構圖。IF、ID、EX、MEM、WB 都在同一週期內完成。

推送至預設分支即建立 submission 並自動評分。請先完成本機測試，再 push。

6.2 What You Need to Implement

Implement a single-cycle CPU supporting the 37 required RV32I instructions.


You may refer to the RV32I Green Card for instruction formats and encodings:

Complete the following nine Verilog modules in rtl/src/:

File Responsibility
Reg_PC.v Store and update the program counter
RegFile.v Implement the register file
Decoder.v Extract instruction fields
Imme_Ext.v Generate the appropriate immediate
ALU.v Perform arithmetic, logical operations, and branch comparisons
JB_Unit.v Calculate jump and branch target sums
LD_Filter.v Select load width and perform sign or zero extension
Controller.v Generate datapath control signals
Top.v Connect the modules and implement the remaining datapath logic

The starter files contain only module and port declarations. You must implement their behavior.

Your CPU must:

  • Preserve x0 as zero.
  • Generate immediates correctly.
  • Distinguish signed and unsigned operations.
  • Select the correct next PC for sequential execution, branches, and jumps.
  • Handle register write-back correctly.
  • Implement byte, halfword, and word loads and stores.
  • Use Top to align data-memory addresses and shift load data, store data, and byte enables.
  • Use an active-low asynchronous reset.

Memory-access assumption

Test programs never perform a load or store that crosses a 32-bit word boundary.

  • Byte accesses may use offsets 0, 1, 2, or 3.
  • Halfword accesses may use offsets 0, 1, or 2.
  • Word accesses use offset 0.

A halfword access at offset 1 is supported in this lab. You do not need to detect cross-word accesses or implement exception handling for them.

Required Instance Names and Memory Connections

Important

Use the exact instance names below inside Top. Names are case-sensitive.

For example, Reg_PC PC (...) instantiates the module Reg_PC with the instance name PC. Do not rename it to pc, u_pc, or another name.

Module Required instance name inside Top
Reg_PC PC
RegFile regfile
SRAM used as instruction memory IM
SRAM used as data memory DM

Declare the register array inside RegFile exactly as follows:

reg [31:0] registers [0:31];

Note

Use the provided support/SRAM.v; you do not need to implement SRAM.

Instantiate it twice: IM with READ_ONLY = 1, and DM with READ_ONLY = 0. You may use the following connections in Top.

SRAM #( .READ_ONLY(1) ) IM ( .clk (clk), .w_en (4'b0000), .address (pc), .write_data (32'b0), .read_data (inst), .halt () ); SRAM #( .READ_ONLY(0) ) DM ( .clk (clk), .w_en (dm_wmask), .address (dm_addr), .write_data (dm_wdata), .read_data (dm_rdata), .halt (halt) );

The signals in this example have the following meanings. Declare and connect them to your datapath.

Signal Width Meaning
pc 32 bits Current instruction address from PC
inst 32 bits Instruction read from IM
dm_addr 32 bits Data-memory byte address with its lowest two bits cleared
dm_wmask 4 bits Store byte enables, shifted according to the byte offset; zero during reset and for non-store instructions
dm_wdata 32 bits Store data shifted into the selected byte lanes
dm_rdata 32 bits Word read from DM, before load-data shifting and filtering

These wire names are examples; the required instance names PC, regfile, IM, and DM must remain unchanged.

Important

Connect DM.halt directly to the halt output of Top.

The provided SRAM asserts this signal when the program performs the termination store. Leave IM.halt unconnected, as shown above.
You do not need to implement ECALL.

Implementation Rules

Warning

Keep the provided infrastructure unchanged.

Implement your CPU in the nine provided files under rtl/src/. Do not modify support/SRAM.v, the CrossVerify framework, CMake files, test programs, or submodules unless explicitly instructed by a TA.

Do not disable verification checks, remove tests, or alter the reference model to hide an implementation error.

Note

Grading uses the TA-provided verification environment.

The program grader takes only the nine submitted files in rtl/src/ and tests them with the TA’s verification framework. Local changes to supporting files will not be used for grading.

TAs grade report.md and its referenced diagram separately.

07CPU 基礎：單週期、PC、RegFile 與記憶體

先完成時序元件：rst=0 非同步清零，PC 與暫存器在上升緣更新；組合路徑在兩個上升緣之間運算。x0 永遠為零，x2 不要另設非零初值。

1. Datapath and Control

A processor can be conceptually divided into two major parts:

  • Datapath: moves and processes data.
  • Control: generates control signals that determine how the datapath should behave for the current instruction.

The datapath contains hardware components such as:

  • Program Counter (PC)
  • Register File
  • ALU
  • Instruction Memory
  • Data Memory
  • Immediate Generator
  • Multiplexers

The controller examines the instruction and determines which datapath operations should be performed.

For example, an add instruction should:

Read rs1 and rs2 ↓ ALU ↓ Add ↓ Write rd

while an lw instruction requires:

Read rs1 ↓ Address = rs1 + immediate ↓ Data Memory ↓ Write rd

Although these instructions use different parts of the datapath, we try to reuse the same hardware whenever possible.

2. What Is a Single-Cycle Processor?

A single-cycle processor completes one instruction in one clock cycle.

During one cycle:

  1. Current state values are read from state elements.
  2. Combinational logic processes these values.
  3. The resulting values become stable before the next rising clock edge.
  4. At the next rising edge, the state elements are updated.

Therefore:

Rising Edge │ │ Instruction executes through combinational logic │ ▼ Next Rising Edge

附件未包含此原圖檔；請依本章的文字、表格與訊號連線說明閱讀。image

One instruction is completed between two consecutive rising clock edges.

This does not mean that every hardware component finishes its work at the same time.

Instead, signals propagate through multiple combinational logic blocks during the cycle until the final values become stable.

2.1 Five Phases of Instruction Execution

It is useful to divide instruction execution into five conceptual phases:

Phase Name Main Function
IF Instruction Fetch Fetch the instruction and determine the next PC
ID Instruction Decode Decode the instruction and read registers
EX Execute Perform an ALU operation or comparison
MEM Memory Access Read or write data memory
WB Write Back Write a result into the Register File

In a single-cycle CPU, these are phases within the same clock cycle.

They are not five separate clock cycles.

Later, in a pipelined CPU, these phases become pipeline stages.

Not every instruction uses every phase.

For example:

Instruction IF ID EX MEM WB
add ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
lw ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
sw ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
beq ✓ ✓ ✓

3. State Elements

A CPU contains two kinds of hardware:

  • State elements, which store information across clock cycles.
  • Combinational logic, which computes values from current inputs.

The main state elements in our datapath are:

PC Register File Instruction Memory Data Memory

3.1 Program Counter


The Program Counter (PC) is a 32-bit register that contains the address of the instruction being executed.

For normal sequential execution:

next_pc = pc + 4

because each RV32I instruction occupies 4 bytes.

The PC is updated on the rising edge of the clock.

For branches and jumps, next_pc may instead be a branch or jump target.

Lab Module to Implement: Reg_PC

In this lab, implement the program counter described above in rtl/src/Reg_PC.v. This is a sequential module with an active-low asynchronous reset.

Port Direction Width Description
clk Input 1 bit Clock. When reset is inactive, update the PC on each rising edge.
rst Input 1 bit Active-low asynchronous reset. Set current_pc to zero when rst = 0, without waiting for a clock edge.
next_pc Input 32 bits Next instruction byte address selected by the datapath in Top.
current_pc Output 32 bits Stored address of the current instruction; used for instruction fetch and PC-relative calculations.

3.2 Register File


RV32I contains 32 general-purpose registers:

x0, x1, ..., x31

The Register File provides:

Two read ports: rs1 → rdata1 rs2 → rdata2 One write port: rd ← wdata

Read

Register reads behave like combinational logic.

As long as rs1 and rs2 are valid, then rdata1 and rdata2 are valid after access time, regardless of what RegWEn is set to.

Write

Rising-edge-triggered write. On rising clock edge, if RegWEn is set to 1, write wdata to R[rd].

Therefore, an instruction can read source registers during the cycle and prepare a result that is written into rd at the next rising edge.

Lab Module to Implement: RegFile

In this lab, implement the two-read-port, one-write-port register file in rtl/src/RegFile.v. Reads are combinational; writes occur on the rising clock edge.

Port Direction Width Description
clk Input 1 bit Clock for register writes.
rst Input 1 bit Active-low asynchronous reset. Clear all 32 registers to zero when rst = 0.
wb_en Input 1 bit Write-back enable, corresponding to the conceptual RegWEn. When high and reset is inactive, write wb_data to the selected destination on the rising edge, except for x0.
wb_data Input 32 bits Value selected by the write-back logic in Top.
rd_index Input 5 bits Destination register index, from 0 to 31.
rs1_index Input 5 bits Register index for the first read port.
rs2_index Input 5 bits Register index for the second read port.
rs1_data_out Output 32 bits Current value of the register selected by rs1_index.
rs2_data_out Output 32 bits Current value of the register selected by rs2_index.

Register x0 must always read as zero. Register reads do not depend on wb_en. The runtime initializes the stack pointer; do not give x2 a special nonzero reset value.

3.3 Instruction Memory and Data Memory

The processor needs memory for two different purposes during one instruction:

  • Fetch an instruction
  • Access program data

For conceptual simplicity, the datapath separates these into:

Instruction Memory (IMEM)

PC → IMEM → instruction

IMEM is read-only during instruction execution.

Its read operation behaves like combinational logic.

Data Memory (DMEM)

DMEM is used by load and store instructions.

Load: address → DMEM → data Store: address + write data → DMEM

DMEM reads behave like combinational logic, while writes occur on the rising clock edge.

This allows the CPU to fetch an instruction and access data memory within the same cycle.

Although both memories are implemented using the same SRAM module, they are instantiated as two independent hardware blocks.

08資料路徑：Decoder、Imme_Ext、ALU、JB_Unit、LD_Filter

依指令類型逐步擴充：R-type → immediate → load/store → branch → jump → U-type。Decoder 的 opcode 僅為 inst[6:2]，func7 只取 inst[30]；不可直接視為完整 ISA 欄位。

4. Building the Datapath

Instead of designing separate hardware for every instruction, we progressively build one datapath and reuse hardware for different instruction types.

We start from the simplest arithmetic instruction and then extend the datapath.

4.1 R-Type Instructions

Consider:

add rd, rs1, rs2

The operation is:

R[rd] = R[rs1] + R[rs2]

The datapath performs:

1. Instruction Fetch

The PC provides the address of the current instruction to the instruction memory.

PC → IMEM → instruction

At the same time, the processor prepares the address of the next sequential instruction:

next_pc = pc + 4

The new PC value will be written at the next rising clock edge.

2. Instruction Decode

The instruction fields select the source and destination registers，:

rd = inst[11:7] rs1 = inst[19:15] rs2 = inst[24:20]

The Register File then outputs:

R[rs1] R[rs2]

Note

In this lab, the Instruction Decode operation is implemented by the Decoder module.


The Decoder receives the complete 32-bit instruction inst[31:0] and extracts:

  • opcode, func3, and func7 → used to determine the instruction operation and generate control signals.
  • rs1_index and rs2_index → used to read source registers from the Register File.
  • rd_index → identifies the destination register for write-back.
    Although different instruction formats use different fields, the Decoder extracts these fields directly from their fixed positions in the instruction.
    Lab Module to Implement: Decoder

In this lab, implement instruction-field extraction in rtl/src/Decoder.v. This module is combinational.

Port Direction Width Description
inst Input 32 bits Complete instruction read from instruction memory.
dc_out_opcode Output 5 bits Instruction operation class: inst[6:2]. This interface omits the lowest two bits of the 7-bit ISA opcode.
dc_out_func3 Output 3 bits Function field inst[14:12], used to distinguish operations within an instruction class.
dc_out_func7 Output 1 bit Instruction bit inst[30], used to distinguish operations such as ADD/SUB and SRL/SRA. This port is not the full 7-bit funct7 field.
dc_out_rs1_index Output 5 bits First source register index: inst[19:15].
dc_out_rs2_index Output 5 bits Second source register index: inst[24:20].
dc_out_rd_index Output 5 bits Destination register index: inst[11:7].

Extract these fields from their fixed bit positions. The other modules determine whether each extracted field is used by the current instruction.

3. Execute

The two source-register values are sent to the ALU.

For an add instruction:

ALUResult = R[rs1] + R[rs2]

4. Memory

add does not access data memory, so this phase is unused.

5. Write Back

The ALU result is connected to the Register File write-data input.

With RegWEn = 1, the result is written into R[rd] at the next rising clock edge.

Supporting Multiple R-Type Operations

sub, and, or, xor, shifts, and comparisons use almost the same datapath.

Only the ALU operation changes.

Therefore, instead of adding another arithmetic unit for every instruction, the controller generates an ALUSel signal:

ALUSel │ ▼ R[rs1] ───────────► ALU ───► ALUResult R[rs2] ───────────►

For example:

add → ALUSel = Add sub → ALUSel = Sub and → ALUSel = AND

The actual encoding of ALUSel is an implementation choice and is not defined by the RISC-V ISA.

Lab Module to Implement: ALU

In this lab, implement the arithmetic and logic unit in rtl/src/ALU.v. The same combinational module also calculates load/store effective addresses and evaluates the branch conditions introduced later.

Port Direction Width Description
opcode Input 5 bits Instruction operation class, corresponding to inst[6:2].
func3 Input 3 bits Instruction function field, corresponding to inst[14:12].
func7 Input 1 bit Instruction bit inst[30], used only where applicable to distinguish operations such as ADD/SUB and SRL/SRA. For other instructions, this bit should not be interpreted as a function bit. This port is not the full 7-bit funct7 field.
operand1 Input 32 bits First operand selected by Top, from rs1_data or the current PC.
operand2 Input 32 bits Second operand selected by Top, from rs2_data or the generated immediate.
alu_out Output 32 bits Arithmetic/logic result, load/store effective byte address, or operand 2 for LUI. Register comparison instructions produce a 32-bit result of 0 or 1 here.
jump Output 1 bit Branch comparison result: 1 when the current branch condition is satisfied, otherwise 0. Set it to 0 for non-branch instructions; JAL and JALR are selected unconditionally by the Controller.

4.2 Instructions with Immediates

Consider:

addi rd, rs1, imm

The operation is:

R[rd] = R[rs1] + imm

The datapath for addi is very similar to the R-Type datapath:

  • The PC still advances to pc + 4.
  • rs1 is still read from the Register File.
  • The result is still written to rd.
  • The same ALU can still perform the addition.

The main difference is the second ALU operand:

R-Type: ALU B = R[rs2] I-Type: ALU B = immediate

Therefore, we do not need another ALU. Instead, we extend the existing datapath so that ALU input B can select between a register value and an immediate value.

We therefore add two components:

  1. A new mux selects the ALU input B based on a new control signal BSel.

    • Set BSel to 1 to pass in the immediate imm.
    • Set Bsel to 0 to pass in the register value R[rs2].

  2. A new block, the immediate generator, generates a 32-bit value imm from the instruction bits inst.

This allows the same ALU to support both:

R-Type: R[rs1] op R[rs2] I-Type: R[rs1] op immediate

Tracing an addi Instruction

The datapath becomes:

Consider:

addi rd, rs1, imm

The processor performs the following operations within one clock cycle.

  1. Instruction Fetch: Increment PC to next instruction (see R-Type datapath). Read the instruction inst from IMEM.

  2. Instruction Decode:

  • Read R[rs1] from RegFile (see R-Type).
  • Set up the destination register rd for writing.
  • Build the immediate imm. For I-Type instructions, wire the upper 12 bits of the instruction inst[31:20] to the input to the Immediate Generator block.
  • Configure control logic.
    • Configure ImmSel to I-type immediates (for now, we only have one type of immediate).
    • Set RegWEn to 1.
    • Set BSel to 1.
    • Set ALUSel to Add.
      After some delay, the immediate generator block’s output signal imm is updated to the appropriate sign-extended 32-bit immediate value, register value R[rs1] is read, and control signals are set.

  1. Execute: Because the control line BSel=1 selects the generated immediate imm for ALU input B, our ALU computes R[rs1] + imm.

  2. Memory: (We don’t access DMEM, so skip this.)

  3. Write Back: Write ALU output to the destination register by connecting alu to RegFile’s wdata input (see R-Type).

    Around the next rising clock edge, wdata, RegWEn, and rd should be held stable through setup and hold time of RegFile.

Note: The Register File still reads rs2.

Register-file reads are combinational and are not explicitly turned off.
Even for addi, inst[24:20] may still select a second register and the Register File may still produce R[rs2].

However, because BSel selects the immediate input, the R[rs2] value is simply ignored.

Immediate Generator

The Immediate Generator (ImmGen) is a combinational logic block.

Its purpose is to reconstruct a 32-bit immediate value from the current 32-bit instruction.

The generated immediate depends on two things:

  1. The instruction format
  2. The positions of the immediate bits inside the instruction

The control signal ImmSel tells ImmGen which immediate format should be generated.

Conceptually:

ImmSel Immediate Format
I I-Type
S S-Type
B B-Type
U U-Type
J J-Type

The exact binary encoding of ImmSel is an implementation choice.

Immediate Formats

The immediate bits are not stored in the same positions for every format.

Therefore, ImmGen must:

  1. Select the appropriate instruction bits.
  2. Rearrange them when necessary.
  3. Insert implicit zero bits when required.
  4. Generate the corresponding 32-bit immediate.

Note

The RISC-V specification explains that register fields are kept in the same positions across instruction formats to simplify register decoding, at the cost of splitting and rearranging immediate bits across formats. The sign bit for all immediates is located at inst[31], allowing sign extension to proceed in parallel with instruction decoding. RISC-V Specification

Lab Module to Implement: Imme_Ext

In this lab, implement the immediate generator in rtl/src/Imme_Ext.v. This module is combinational and determines the immediate format from the instruction itself.

Port Direction Width Description
inst Input 32 bits Complete instruction. Use its opcode to select the I-, S-, B-, U-, or J-Type immediate format.
imm_ext_out Output 32 bits Reconstructed immediate: sign-extended for I/S/B/J formats, with the implicit low zero bit included for B/J; for U-Type, inst[31:12] followed by 12 zero bits.

Although the conceptual explanation uses ImmSel, this lab module has no ImmSel input. Decode the format internally from inst. The output is used as an ALU operand or as the offset input to JB_Unit.

4.3 Load and Store Instructions

Loads and stores introduce Data Memory (DMEM) into the datapath.

1. Load

Consider:

lw rd, imm(rs1)

The effective memory address is:

address = R[rs1] + imm

Therefore, the ALU is reused as an address calculator.

A new write-back MUX is required because data written to rd may now come from:

ALU result or DMEM output

The control signal WBSel determines the source.

2. Store

We do not need to add additional blocks for stores, but we will need to:

  1. Upgrade the Immediate Generator to support immediates in S-Type instructions; we encourage you to read that section afterwards.
  2. Wire R[rs2] to wdata (DMEM input signal).

Partial Loads and Stores

The data memory used in this lab accesses data in 32-bit words. However, RISC-V also supports byte and halfword load/store instructions.

Therefore, the processor must determine which bytes inside a 32-bit memory word are actually used.

In this lab, partial load/store operations are handled by the existing datapath:

  • Top handles the byte position inside an aligned 32-bit SRAM word.
  • LD_Filter handles load width and sign/zero extension.
  • Controller determines the store width and generates the basic byte write-enable signal.

1. Word-Aligned Memory Access

Although memory is byte-addressed, each SRAM access operates on one 32-bit word, or four consecutive bytes.

A valid SRAM access therefore begins at an address that is a multiple of 4:

Word Address Bytes Accessed
0 0, 1, 2, 3
4 4, 5, 6, 7
8 8, 9, 10, 11
12 12, 13, 14, 15

The ALU still calculates the complete effective byte address:

effective_address = R[rs1] + imm

The address is then used in two ways:

  • The upper address bits select the aligned 32-bit SRAM word.
  • effective_address[1:0] identifies the byte position inside that word.

For example:

  • address[1:0] = 00: byte 0
  • address[1:0] = 01: byte 1
  • address[1:0] = 10: byte 2
  • address[1:0] = 11: byte 3

The lower two address bits are therefore not part of the SRAM word address, but they are still required for partial load/store operations.

2. Memory Access Assumption

In this lab, we assume that a single load or store instruction never crosses a 32-bit word boundary.

Therefore:

  • lw and sw use addresses whose lower two bits are 00.
  • lh, lhu, and sh may only be used when all required bytes remain inside the same 32-bit word.
  • lb, lbu, and sb may start at any byte offset.

For example, an lh starting at byte 9 accesses bytes 9 and 10, which are both inside the aligned word containing bytes 8–11.

An lh starting at byte 11 would require bytes 11 and 12 and would cross a word boundary, so this case is not considered in this lab.

3. Partial Loads

For every load instruction, SRAM reads the entire aligned 32-bit word.

Top first uses effective_address[1:0] to select the requested byte or halfword and move it to the least significant bits of the load data.

The resulting 32-bit value is then sent to LD_Filter.

LD_Filter uses func3 to determine the load type:

func3 Instruction Operation in LD_Filter
000 lb Sign-extend ld_data[7:0]
001 lh Sign-extend ld_data[15:0]
010 lw Use all 32 bits
100 lbu Zero-extend ld_data[7:0]
101 lhu Zero-extend ld_data[15:0]

Therefore, partial load handling is divided into two steps:

  1. Top selects the correct byte position using address[1:0].
  2. LD_Filter performs the required sign extension or zero extension.

The byte offset determines which part of the SRAM output is moved to the least significant bits before entering LD_Filter.

Instruction address[1:0] Data selected from SRAM
lb, lbu 00 read_data[7:0]
lb, lbu 01 read_data[15:8]
lb, lbu 10 read_data[23:16]
lb, lbu 11 read_data[31:24]
lh, lhu 00 read_data[15:0]
lh, lhu 01 read_data[23:8]
lh, lhu 10 read_data[31:16]
lw 00 read_data[31:0]

After the required data is moved to the least significant bits, LD_Filter performs the final extension.

Example: lb at Address 6

Suppose an lb instruction accesses byte address 6.

The SRAM reads the aligned word containing:

4, 5, 6, 7

Since:

address[1:0] = 10

the requested byte is:

read_data[23:16]

Top moves this byte to ld_data[7:0].

Then LD_Filter recognizes func3 = 000 and sign-extends ld_data[7:0] to 32 bits.

The final result is written back to the destination register.

Example: lh at Address 9

Suppose an lh instruction accesses byte address 9.

The SRAM reads the aligned word containing:

8, 9, 10, 11

Since:

address[1:0] = 01

the requested halfword is:

read_data[23:8]

Top moves these 16 bits to ld_data[15:0].

Then LD_Filter recognizes func3 = 001 and sign-extends ld_data[15:0] to 32 bits.

Lab Module to Implement: LD_Filter

In this lab, implement load-width selection and extension in rtl/src/LD_Filter.v. This module is combinational and receives load data after Top has applied the byte-offset shift.

Port Direction Width Description
func3 Input 3 bits Load type: 000 for LB, 001 for LH, 010 for LW, 100 for LBU, and 101 for LHU.
ld_data Input 32 bits SRAM read data shifted by Top so that the requested byte or halfword starts at bit 0.
ld_data_f Output 32 bits Final load value for write-back: sign-extend the low 8/16 bits for LB/LH, zero-extend them for LBU/LHU, or pass all 32 bits for LW.

LD_Filter has no address input and does not select a byte lane by itself. Byte-position handling belongs in Top.

4. Partial Stores

For store instructions, SRAM also accesses one aligned 32-bit word.

However, sb and sh should modify only part of that word.

The Controller first determines the store width according to func3 and generates a basic 4-bit byte write-enable signal.

Instruction func3 Basic w_en
sb 000 0001
sh 001 0011
sw 010 1111

When the current instruction should not write to Data Memory:

w_en = 4'b0000

The basic w_en specifies how many bytes should be written, but it does not yet specify their final byte positions inside the aligned 32-bit SRAM word.

Top uses effective_address[1:0] to place both the store data and the write-enable bits in the correct byte lanes.

Therefore, partial store handling is divided into two steps:

  1. Controller determines the store width and generates the basic w_en.
  2. Top shifts rs2_data and w_en according to effective_address[1:0].

Each bit of the final w_en controls one byte of the 32-bit SRAM word:

Write Enable SRAM Byte
w_en[0] write_data[7:0]
w_en[1] write_data[15:8]
w_en[2] write_data[23:16]
w_en[3] write_data[31:24]

If a bit of w_en is 0, the corresponding SRAM byte is not modified.

Store Width Generated by Controller
Instruction Basic w_en Store Data
sb 0001 rs2_data[7:0]
sh 0011 rs2_data[15:0]
sw 1111 rs2_data[31:0]
Byte Position Handling in Top

For sb:

address[1:0] Final w_en
00 0001
01 0010
10 0100
11 1000

For sh:

address[1:0] Final w_en
00 0011
01 0110
10 1100

For sw, the address offset is 00, so:

w_en = 4'b1111

Conceptually, Top performs:

final_w_en = basic_w_en << effective_address[1:0]

The store data is shifted by the same number of byte positions:

write_data = rs2_data << (8 × effective_address[1:0])

Example: sb at Address 3

Suppose an sb instruction stores to byte address 3.

The Controller identifies sb and generates:

basic_w_en = 4'b0001

Since:

address[1:0] = 11

Top shifts the write-enable mask by three byte positions:

final_w_en = 4'b1000

The lowest byte of rs2_data is also moved to:

write_data[31:24]

Therefore, only byte 3 of the aligned SRAM word is modified.

Example: sh at Address 2

Suppose an sh instruction stores to byte address 2.

The Controller identifies sh and generates:

basic_w_en = 4'b0011

Since:

address[1:0] = 10

Top shifts the write-enable mask by two byte positions:

final_w_en = 4'b1100

The lowest 16 bits of rs2_data are also moved to:

write_data[31:16]

Therefore, only bytes 2 and 3 are modified.

Store instructions do not perform sign extension.

sb uses the lowest 8 bits of rs2_data, sh uses the lowest 16 bits, and sw uses all 32 bits.

Implementation Summary

The ALU first computes the effective byte address:

effective_address = R[rs1] + imm

The upper address bits select the aligned 32-bit SRAM word, while:

effective_address[1:0]

determines the byte position inside that word.

Partial memory accesses are handled by the existing datapath:

  • Top

    • Converts the effective byte address to the aligned SRAM word address.
    • Uses address[1:0] to position load/store data inside the 32-bit word.
    • Shifts the store write-enable mask to the correct byte lanes.

  • LD_Filter

    • Handles lb, lh, lw, lbu, and lhu.
    • Performs sign extension or zero extension after the requested load data has been moved to the least significant bits.

  • Controller

    • Detects sb, sh, and sw.
    • Generates the basic byte write-enable according to the store width:
      • sb: 0001
      • sh: 0011
      • sw: 1111
    • Generates 0000 when Data Memory should not be written.

4.4 Supporting Branches

Branch instructions may change the next PC depending on the result of a comparison between two registers.

For example:

beq rs1, rs2, imm

performs two operations:

  • Compare R[rs1] and R[rs2].
  • If they are equal, jump to pc + imm; otherwise continue to pc + 4.

Therefore, supporting branch instructions requires the datapath to:

  1. Compare rs1 and rs2.
  2. Calculate the branch target address.
  3. Select the correct next PC.

1. ALU Input Selection

The ALU can receive different operand sources depending on the instruction, so multiplexers are placed before its inputs.

For a branch instruction, the ALU must compare the two register values:

  • ALU operand 1 selects rs1_data.
  • ALU operand 2 selects rs2_data.

The ALU then performs the comparison required by func3.

Instruction Branch Condition
beq rs1 == rs2
bne rs1 != rs2
blt signed rs1 < rs2
bge signed rs1 >= rs2
bltu unsigned rs1 < rs2
bgeu unsigned rs1 >= rs2

The purpose of these multiplexers is to allow the same ALU to be reused by different instruction types.

For example, some instructions require the ALU to use pc or an immediate value, while a branch instruction requires both register values.

2. Calculating the Branch Target

While the ALU compares rs1 and rs2, the branch target must also be calculated:

branch_target = pc + imm

In this lab, this calculation is performed by the JB_Unit.

A multiplexer is placed before the first input of the JB_Unit so that the same unit can also support jump instructions.

pcMUXrs1_datajb_op1_seljb_in1JB Unitimmout 31:0jb_pc

For branch instructions:

jb_op1_sel → pc

so the JB_Unit calculates:

jb_pc = pc + sext_imme

For jalr, the same MUX can instead select rs1_data, allowing the JB_Unit to generate a target based on rs1 + imm.

Therefore, the MUX allows the same JB_Unit to be reused for different control-transfer instructions.

Lab Module to Implement: JB_Unit

In this lab, implement the jump/branch target adder in rtl/src/JB_Unit.v. This combinational module computes a sum while the ALU can independently evaluate a branch condition.

Port Direction Width Description
operand1 Input 32 bits Target base selected by Top: the current PC for branches and JAL, or rs1_data for JALR.
operand2 Input 32 bits Immediate offset generated by Imme_Ext for the current branch or jump.
jb_out Output 32 bits 32-bit sum of operand1 and operand2, used to form the branch or jump target.

JB_Unit only adds its inputs. Top clears bit 0 of the sum for JALR and selects whether the PC takes this target or advances by 4.

3. Selecting the Next PC

The processor has two possible next addresses during a branch instruction:

  • pc + 4: continue to the next instruction.
  • jb_pc: go to the branch target.

The branch comparison result determines which one is selected.

If the branch condition is false: next_pc = pc + 4

If the branch condition is true: next_pc = jb_pc

The next_pc_sel signal controls the MUX before the PC.

Branch Datapath Summary

For a branch instruction:

  • The ALU input MUXes select rs1_data and rs2_data.
  • The ALU determines whether the branch condition is satisfied.
  • The MUX before JB_Unit selects pc.
  • JB_Unit calculates pc + imm.
  • next_pc_sel selects between pc + 4 and jb_pc.

No Data Memory access or Register File write-back is required.

4.5 Supporting Jumps

RISC-V provides two unconditional jump instructions:

  • jal — Jump and Link
  • jalr — Jump and Link Register

Unlike a branch, a jump does not need to check a condition. The processor always changes the PC to the jump target.

At the same time, both instructions write pc + 4 to rd, so that the program can return to the instruction after the jump.

1. Calculating the Jump Target

The JB_Unit is reused to calculate the jump target.

A MUX before the JB_Unit selects whether the first operand comes from pc or rs1_data.

pcMUXrs1_datajb_op1_seljb_in1JB Unitimmout 31:0jb_pc

The least significant bit of the jalr target is cleared to 0.This guarantees at least 2-byte alignment and allows the least significant bit of a function pointer to be used for auxiliary information.

Instruction JB Unit Input 1 Jump Target
jal pc pc + imm
jalr rs1_data (rs1_data + imm) & ~1

2. Writing the Return Address

The dedicated adder next to the PC continuously calculates: pc + 4

For both jal and jalr, the write-back MUX selects this value and writes it to rd: R[rd] = pc + 4

At the same time, the PC selects jb_pc as the next instruction address.

No Data Memory access is required.

4.6 Supporting U-Type Instructions

RV32I contains two U-Type instructions:

  • lui — Load Upper Immediate
  • auipc — Add Upper Immediate to PC

Both instructions use a U-Type immediate: imm = {inst[31:12], 12'b0}

Therefore, the Immediate Generator must support the U-Type format.

1. lui

lui writes the U-Type immediate directly into the destination register: R[rd] = imm

No register operand is required.

In this lab, the immediate is selected as the second ALU operand, and the ALU supports passing this operand directly to its output.

2. auipc

auipc adds the U-Type immediate to the current PC: R[rd] = pc + imm

The ALU input MUXes therefore select:

  • operand 1: pc
  • operand 2: imm

and the ALU performs:

ALU output = pc + imm

The result is written to rd.

U-Type Datapath Summary

Instruction ALU Operand 1 ALU Operand 2 ALU Operation Result
lui Don't care imm Pass operand 2 R[rd] = imm
auipc pc imm Add R[rd] = pc + imm

Neither instruction accesses Data Memory, and the next PC remains: pc + 4

09Controller 與 Top 整合：控制訊號、寫回與下一個 PC

Controller 產生選擇訊號，Top 完成 MUX 與記憶體 byte lane 定位。JAL/JALR 寫回 PC+4；JALR 目標清除 bit 0。PC、regfile、IM、DM 的 instance 名稱不可變更。

5. Control Logic

By progressively adding support for R-Type, immediate, load/store, branch, jump, and U-Type instructions, we obtain the complete datapath shown below.

Important

The complete datapath shown above is also the CPU architecture that you will implement in this lab.

The datapath now contains all hardware required to execute the supported instructions.

However, different instructions use the same hardware in different ways.

For example:

  • The ALU inputs may come from registers, the PC, or an immediate.
  • The JB_Unit may use either pc or rs1_data.
  • The next PC may be pc + 4 or jb_pc.
  • The value written back to rd may come from alu_out, ld_data_f, or pc + 4.
  • Data Memory should only be written by store instructions.

The Controller determines these choices according to the current instruction.

5.1 Control Signals

附件未包含此原圖檔；請依本章的文字、表格與訊號連線說明閱讀。image

The Controller receives the decoded instruction information:

  • opcode
  • func3
  • func7

and generates the control signals required by the datapath.

Control Signal Purpose
next_pc_sel Selects pc + 4 or jb_pc as next_pc
im_w_en Controls writing to Instruction Memory
wb_en Enables writing to the Register File
jb_op1_sel Selects pc or rs1_data as the first operand of JB_Unit
alu_op1_sel Selects the first ALU operand
alu_op2_sel Selects the second ALU operand
wb_sel Selects the source of wb_data
dm_w_en Controls which bytes of Data Memory are written

The ALU operation itself is determined by:

  • opcode
  • func3
  • func7

The exact binary encoding of the select signals is an implementation choice.

For the following table:

  • Reg means register data.
  • Imm means the generated immediate.
  • JB means jb_pc.
  • Mem means ld_data_f.
  • * means don't care, because that hardware result is not used by the instruction.

Lab Module to Implement: Controller

In this lab, implement the combinational control logic in rtl/src/Controller.v. It receives the decoded instruction fields and the ALU branch result, and generates the following outputs.

Port Direction Width Description
opcode Input 5 bits Decoded instruction operation class, inst[6:2].
func3 Input 3 bits Decoded function field, inst[14:12].
func7 Input 1 bit Decoded instruction bit inst[30], not the full funct7 field.
jump Input 1 bit Branch condition result from the ALU. Use it when deciding whether a conditional branch is taken.
next_pc_sel Output 1 bit Next-PC selection: 0 selects pc + 4; 1 selects the branch/jump target. Select the target for a taken branch, JAL, or JALR.
im_w_en Output 4 bits Instruction-memory byte write enables. Keep this output at 0000 because instructions are read-only during execution.
wb_en Output 1 bit Register write-back enable. Assert for instructions that write rd; deassert for stores and branches.
jb_op1_sel Output 1 bit Selects the current PC or rs1_data as the first input of JB_Unit.
alu_op1_sel Output 1 bit Selects the current PC or rs1_data as ALU operand 1.
alu_op2_sel Output 1 bit Selects the generated immediate or rs2_data as ALU operand 2.
alu_opcode Output 5 bits Operation-class information for the ALU; forward opcode for this interface.
alu_func3 Output 3 bits Function information for the ALU; forward func3.
alu_func7 Output 1 bit Operation-distinguishing bit for the ALU; forward func7.
wb_sel Output 1 bit Selects load data versus the non-load write-back path. In the non-load path, Top distinguishes ALU results from the pc + 4 link value required by JAL/JALR.
dm_w_en Output 4 bits Unshifted store byte-enable mask: 0001 for SB, 0011 for SH, 1111 for SW, and 0000 for non-store instructions. Top shifts this mask by the byte offset.

5.2 Control Signal Table

Instruction next_pc_sel im_w_en wb_en jb_op1_sel alu_op1_sel alu_op2_sel ALU Operation wb_sel dm_w_en
R-Type PC+4 0000 1 * rs1 rs2 func3/func7 ALU 0000
I-Type PC+4 0000 1 * rs1 imm func3/func7 ALU 0000
Load PC+4 0000 1 * rs1 imm ADD MEM 0000
Store PC+4 0000 0 * rs1 imm ADD * func3
Branch depends on result 0000 0 pc rs1 rs2 Compare * 0000
jal JB 0000 1 pc * * * PC+4 0000
jalr JB 0000 1 rs1 * * * PC+4 0000
lui PC+4 0000 1 * * imm Pass op2 ALU 0000
auipc PC+4 0000 1 * pc imm ADD ALU 0000

For store instructions, the basic Data Memory write-enable is determined by func3:

Instruction func3 Basic dm_w_en
sb 000 0001
sh 001 0011
sw 010 1111

The basic write-enable is then shifted according to effective_address[1:0], as discussed in the Partial Stores section.

5.3 Branch Control

Most control signals depend only on the instruction itself.

Branch instructions are different because the next PC also depends on the comparison result.

The ALU compares rs1_data and rs2_data and produces the branch result jump.

Therefore: next_pc_sel = 1, when a branch is taken, or for jal and jalr.

Otherwise: next_pc_sel = 0 and the processor continues with:

pc + 4

Conceptually:

Instruction Condition Next PC
Normal instruction — pc + 4
Branch not taken jump = 0 pc + 4
Branch taken jump = 1 jb_pc
jal Always jb_pc
jalr Always jb_pc

5.4 Write-Back Control

Instructions that write to the Register File may obtain their result from three different sources:

Instruction Type Write-Back Source
R-Type alu_out
I-Type ALU alu_out
lui alu_out
auipc alu_out
Load ld_data_f
jal, jalr pc + 4

Therefore, the final write-back MUX has three inputs:

alu_out

ld_data_f

pc + 4

and wb_sel determines which value becomes wb_data.

Store and branch instructions do not write to the Register File, so: wb_en = 0. For instructions that write a result to rd: wb_en = 1.

5.5 Complete Single-Cycle CPU Architecture

附件未包含此原圖檔；請依本章的文字、表格與訊號連線說明閱讀。image

Lab Module to Implement: Top

In this lab, integrate the complete single-cycle datapath in rtl/src/Top.v. Instantiate the CPU modules and the two provided SRAM instances, and implement operand selection, write-back selection, next-PC selection, and partial load/store positioning.

Port Direction Width Description
clk Input 1 bit CPU clock. Connect it to Reg_PC, RegFile, and both SRAM instances.
rst Input 1 bit Active-low asynchronous reset for Reg_PC and RegFile. Keep data-memory write enables at zero while reset is asserted. The provided SRAM has no reset port.
halt Output 1 bit Program-termination indication from DM.halt. Connect it directly to that output of the provided data-memory SRAM; do not drive it from Controller or a separate procedural block.

Top has no external instruction or data-memory ports because both SRAM instances are inside it. Preserve the required instance names PC, regfile, IM, and DM; the memory connections are provided in Section 6.2.

10建置 RTL、參考 ISS 與七項測試程式
git submodule update --init --recursive cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j 4

執行環境：課程容器／Lab3 專案根目錄

目的：依序初始化、設定並建置

預期結果：產生 build/verilator_sim 與測試程式

首次建置包含 Verilator、reference ISS 與 RISC-V 程式。後續修改 RTL，仍必須先 build；CTest 不會自動重新編譯。

ctest --test-dir build -N ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

執行環境：課程容器／Lab3 專案根目錄

目的：列出並執行所有測試

預期結果：成功訊息應為 100% tests passed, 0 tests failed out of 7

這是預期成功訊息，不代表已替你的 CPU 執行並通過測試。
11本機測試與修正循環：CrossVerify → GTKWave

CrossVerify 讓 RTL 與 ISS 各執行一條指令，逐步比對 PC、32 個暫存器與記憶體存取。從第一個 mismatch 找原因，重建後先測失敗項目，最後跑全部七項。

6.3 Verify and Debug Your CPU

After implementing the CPU modules and connecting them in Top.v, follow the steps below to verify your design.

Run all commands inside the course Docker container, from the repository root, where CMakeLists.txt is located.

Warning

Test locally before pushing.

Every push to your assignment repository’s default branch triggers autograding. The grading runners are shared by the entire class and have limited capacity. Use local tests and waveforms to debug your CPU before pushing your changes.

Step 1: Understand What the Tests Check

Each test runs the same RISC-V program on two implementations:

  • Your RTL CPU, simulated using Verilator.
  • The reference ISS, a provided software model of RISC-V instruction execution.

CrossVerify lets both implementations execute one instruction, then compares their PC and all 32 general-purpose registers. It also checks memory-access addresses, store byte enables, store data, and the affected RAM word after a store.

For example, after executing:

addi x5, x0, 10

both implementations should have x5 = 10 and the same next PC. If your CPU produces a different result, CrossVerify reports the mismatch and stops the test.

Same test program ↓ RTL CPU and reference ISS each execute one instruction ↓ CrossVerify compares their execution states ↓ Match: continue to the next instruction Mismatch: report the error and stop

The platform reads your CPU through hierarchical paths such as top.PC.current_pc and top.regfile.registers. Make sure your implementation follows the required hierarchical names.

For C tests, the provided runtime calls terminate() after main() returns. It writes the byte value 1 to 0xFFFFFFFB, causing the provided SRAM to assert DM.halt. Connect this output to Top.halt. CrossVerify checks the final state and verifies that the reference ISS also halted before reporting success. Assembly tests issue the same termination store directly.

You do not need to implement ECALL. The termination store uses your normal store datapath, including address alignment, write-data shifting, and byte enables.

Step 2: Configure and Build the Project

Initialize the reference ISS and runtime submodules:

git submodule update --init --recursive

Configure the project:

cmake -S . -B build

Build the simulator and test programs:

cmake --build build -j 4

The build compiles the reference ISS and RISC-V test programs, and uses Verilator to generate an executable simulator from your RTL. The simulator is created at build/verilator_sim.

Resolve all configuration and build errors before proceeding. Errors mentioning missing names such as top.PC or top.regfile.registers usually indicate that required instances or internal state have not been declared with the expected names.

After later RTL changes, you normally only need to repeat the build command:

cmake --build build -j 4

Step 3: Run the Tests

List the available tests:

ctest --test-dir build -N

You should see these seven tests:

Test Main coverage
print_test Output and memory-mapped I/O
msort_test Merge sort
qsort_test Quick sort
matmul_test Matrix multiplication
malloc_test_test Dynamic memory allocation
isa_edges_test RV32I instruction edge cases
partial_access_test Partial loads/stores, data extension, and byte enables

Run all tests:

ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

CTest launches the simulator for each test program and displays output from failed tests. A successful run ends with:

100% tests passed, 0 tests failed out of 7

If a test fails, continue with the following debugging steps.

Step 4: Locate the Failure Using CrossVerify

Start by reading the failed test’s output. Identify the reported instruction address and the first mismatch.

Reported problem What to inspect first
PC mismatch Next-PC selection, branch condition, jump target, and JALR target alignment
Register mismatch Source operands, immediate generation, ALU result, load result, and writeback control
Memory-address mismatch Effective-address calculation and word alignment
Store-mask or store-data mismatch Store width, byte offset, byte enables, and write-data shifting
RAM mismatch Memory write connections and which bytes were modified

These are starting points for investigation, not guaranteed diagnoses.

To focus on one failing test, run it separately. For example:

ctest --test-dir build -R '^partial_access_test$' --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The -R option selects a test by name. Replace partial_access_test with the name of the test you want to investigate.

CrossVerify tells you which visible result first became incorrect. Use a waveform to trace how your datapath produced that result.

Step 5: Generate and Open a Waveform

After successfully rebuilding your RTL, run the simulator from the repository root with +trace enabled. For example, to trace partial_access_test:

./build/verilator_sim +prog_elf_path=build/tests/partial_access.elf +trace
  • ./build/verilator_sim starts the RTL simulator with CrossVerify enabled.
  • +prog_elf_path=... selects the compiled test program.
  • +trace records the waveform to waveform.fst in the current directory.

To trace a different test, replace the path after +prog_elf_path= using the table below. The CTest name and program filename are not always identical.

Test Program path
print_test build/runtime/test-progs/print
msort_test build/runtime/test-progs/msort
qsort_test build/runtime/test-progs/qsort
matmul_test build/runtime/test-progs/matmul
malloc_test_test build/runtime/test-progs/malloc_test
isa_edges_test build/tests/isa_edges.elf
partial_access_test build/tests/partial_access.elf

For example, to trace qsort_test:

./build/verilator_sim +prog_elf_path=build/runtime/test-progs/qsort +trace

Open the generated waveform in GTKWave:

gtkwave waveform.fst

Each run using +trace from the same directory overwrites waveform.fst. After modifying your RTL, rebuild the simulator and rerun the selected test with +trace to generate an updated waveform.

Step 6: Trace the Incorrect Result in GTKWave

In GTKWave, expand the hierarchy to find CrossVerify and its CPU instance, top. Add the relevant signals to the waveform view.

Start with:

  • clk and rst.
  • PC.current_pc.
  • IM.read_data.
  • The control and datapath signals related to the reported failure.

Find the cycle where PC.current_pc matches the failing instruction address reported by CrossVerify. For this single-cycle CPU, inspect the operands and combinational results before the rising clock edge, then inspect the updated PC, registers, or memory after the edge.

For example, if CrossVerify reports an incorrect register value after an ALU instruction:

  1. Check that IM.read_data contains the expected instruction.
  2. Check the decoded source and destination register indices.
  3. Check the source-register values and generated immediate.
  4. Check which operands reach the ALU and whether its result is correct.
  5. Check the writeback data, destination index, and write enable.
  6. Check the destination register after the rising edge.

For a store failure, inspect the data-memory interface:

Effective address ↓ Word-aligned address and byte offset ↓ Shifted store data and byte enables ↓ DM.address, DM.write_data, and DM.w_en ↓ Memory update at the rising edge

For example, an SB targeting byte offset 3 should select w_en = 4'b1000, with the byte to be written placed in write_data[31:24].

Signal names inside your datapath may differ. Follow the connections in your own Top.v to choose the signals to inspect.

Step 7: Fix, Rebuild, and Verify Again

After modifying your RTL, rebuild:

cmake --build build -j 4

CTest does not rebuild your RTL automatically. Wait for the build to succeed before testing.

Rerun the previously failing test:

ctest --test-dir build -R '^partial_access_test$' --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

If needed, repeat Step 5 to generate a new waveform from the updated implementation.

Once the failure is resolved, run all tests again:

ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

A fix may affect other instructions, so confirm that all seven tests pass before pushing your changes.

6.5 Assignment Report and Classroom50 Submission

Complete the provided report.md. You may write your answers in English or Traditional Chinese.report.md must include CPU architecture diagram: Draw a diagram of your single-cycle CPU showing its modules, main datapath connections, and control signals. You may draw it by hand or use draw.io. Include a clear image in this report.

Before submitting, rebuild and run the complete local test suite:

cmake --build build -j 4 ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

Stage and commit your RTL, report, and diagram. For example, if the diagram is saved as cpu-architecture.png:

git add rtl/src report.md cpu-architecture.png git commit -m "feat: complete Lab 3 single-cycle CPU"

Replace cpu-architecture.png with your actual image path.

Check that the submitted files have no uncommitted changes:

git status --short -- rtl/src report.md cpu-architecture.png

Then push your commit to the default branch of your Classroom50 repository:

git push

Every push to the default branch creates a submission and triggers autograding.

Open the GitHub Actions run and the submission’s autograder details. Confirm that the graded commit matches your final pushed commit.

本作業依附件以預設分支 push 觸發自動評分，不需要另外執行提交命令。只推送已本機測試的版本。

6.6 Final Submission Checklist

Before the deadline, make sure:

  • All nine required .v modules are implemented.
  • All 37 required RV32I instructions are supported.
  • x0 remains zero, and branches and jumps update the PC correctly.
  • Partial loads and stores use the correct byte offsets, data shifts, and byte enables.
  • The required hierarchical names are preserved.
  • The project builds successfully, and all seven local tests pass.
  • Supporting and grading infrastructure has not been modified.
  • report.md contains your name, student ID, architecture diagram, module explanations, and reflection.
  • The diagram image is committed and displays correctly on GitHub.
  • The final RTL, report, and image files are committed.
  • The final commit has been pushed to the default branch before the deadline.
  • The autograding result for that commit has been checked.
